title: Revisiting Group Relative Policy Optimization: Insights into On-Policy and Off-Policy Training
claim: A normalized-variance penalty term stays near its minimum for moderate success rates but diverges as success probability approaches 0 or 1, dominating the bound.
layout: single line plot, U-shaped curve over p from 0 to 1, title above, legend with formula at bottom-left, dashed grid
description: A single matplotlib-style line plot titled 'Plot of (1 - std(X)) / std(X) for Bernoulli(p)'. The x-axis is p from 0 to 1.0 and the y-axis is (1 - std(X))/std(X), running from about 1 to 9. One purple curve forms a symmetric U shape. It sits near 1 around p=0.5, rises slowly toward p=0.2 and p=0.8, then shoots up steeply near p=0 and p=1, reaching about 9 at the plot edges. A small legend at bottom-left shows the formula as a fraction. A light dashed grid covers the plot. The eye goes first to the steep upward edges of the curve, which show the blow-up at extreme success probabilities.
caption: $\frac{1- \sigma_{\alpha,r,\varepsilon}(x)}{\sigma_{\alpha,r,\varepsilon}(x)}$ explodes when variance is zero, meaning for fully correct or wrong policies, this term dominates the lower bound.
abstract: We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in both on-policy and off-policy optimization regimes. Our motivation comes from recent work on off-policy Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which improves training stability, sampling efficiency, and memory usage. In addition, a recent analysis of GRPO suggests that estimating the advantage function with off-policy samples could be beneficial. Building on these observations, we adapt GRPO to the off-policy setting. We show that both on-policy and off-policy GRPO objectives yield an improvement in the reward. This result motivates the use of clipped surrogate objectives in the off-policy version of GRPO. We then compare the empirical performance of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in post-training using both GRPO variants. Our results show that off-policy GRPO either significantly outperforms or performs on par with its on-policy counterpart.
